subject: Culture
title: Bible Translation Wars
description: A quick win: understand Bible Translation Wars.

hook.text: William Tyndale was strangled and burned in 1536 for translating the Bible into English.

buildup.text: The Church argued that only Latin scripture was valid. Vernacular Bibles threatened clerical authority.

discovery.text: Tyndale invented English words to translate Greek: 'scapegoat,' 'atonement,' and 'Passover' are all his.

twist.text: Just 75 years later, King James commissioned an official English Bible using 80% of Tyndale's condemned text.

climax.text: Today the Bible exists in over 700 languages. Each translation carries the translator's theology and politics.

punchline.text: Yesterday's heresy becomes today's standard edition.

quiz.question: Which common English word did William Tyndale coin?

details.summary: Bible translation has been one of the most politically explosive acts in history. William Tyndale was executed for translating the Bible into English. Martin Luther's German translation fueled the Reformation.
details.whyItMatters: Bible translation history proves that translation is never neutral — choosing which words and concepts to use fundamentally shapes how millions understand morality, authority, and truth.
takeaways: William Tyndale was strangled and burned for translating the Bible into English
Luther's German Bible standardized the German language
Missionary translations imposed Christian concepts on Indigenous worldviews

faq.question: Why was Bible translation so dangerous?
faq.answer: The Catholic Church maintained that only clergy could interpret scripture, keeping the Bible in Latin reserved for the educated elite. Translating into vernacular languages gave ordinary people direct access to religious text, bypassing church authority.

faq.question: How did Bible translation affect Indigenous cultures?
faq.answer: Missionaries translating the Bible into Indigenous languages created written forms for previously oral languages — preserving them in one sense. But translation required imposing Christian concepts (sin, salvation, heaven) onto languages without equivalent words, fundamentally restructuring.
